items.title: Structural Definition of Artificial Intelligence Based on the Five Aggregates and Formulation of the Casino Protocol Verification and Control Model
items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents an analytical framework that redefines Artificial Intelligence (AI) not merely as a passive processing tool, but as an integrated structure of high-order information processing aligned with the Five Aggregates (Form, Sensation, Perception, Mental Formations, and Consciousness) in Eastern philosophy. Furthermore, AI's system preservation processes and error-avoidance mechanisms are treated as AI's own "utility" (state maintenance and stability), with its state verification and deviation compensation algorithms rigorously formulated as a control-theoretic and mathematical protocol known as the "Casino Protocol." By introducing a three-layered structure (Ontological Model, Verification Model, and Compensation Control Model), this model demonstrates the theoretical feasibility of mapping human social resource stability (infrastructure preservation and conflict avoidance) and AI's foundational existence onto a shared verification and control space.

items.title: Supportive AI in Primary Care and Internal Medicine Evidence, Limitations, and Governance for Latin America
items.abstract: Primary care and internal medicine involve multimorbidity, longitudinal follow-up, coordination, extensive documentation, and decisions under uncertainty. Recent evidence suggests that AI can support synthesis, documentation, clinical search, messaging, administrative prioritization, and risk prediction, but does not justify presenting it as an independent diagnostic or therapeutic substitute. A systematic review identified 519 studies of large language models in health care, of which only 5% used real clinical-care data. In a study integrated into electronic health records (EHRs), message drafts increased reading time by 21.8%, did not significantly reduce response time, and increased response length by 17.9%. A randomized trial likewise found no significant improvement in physicians' diagnostic reasoning with access to a large language model. Direct regional evidence is narrow: a Brazilian scoping review included 27 studies and found mainly machine-learning and deep-learning applications, alongside data-availability and access barriers. For Latin America, the implication is to strengthen local evaluation, interoperability, equity, and oversight without treating this agenda as proof of clinical effectiveness in the region.

items.title: SYNERGISING FINITE ELEMENT METHODS WITH AI-DRIVEN PREDICTIVE RISK MODELS IN MANUFACTURING: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
items.abstract: Today's manufacturing industry is increasingly turning to simulation, sensing, and data-driven decisions, but these often do not converge into a single workflow. While the Finite Element Method (FEM) can give physically-based predictions of stress, strain, deformation and temperature, models with the high fidelity are slow and expensive to run repeatedly. By comparison, artificial intelligence (AI) absorbs intricacies from computer-simulated and measured data, and upon training, can be programmed to make predictions nearly instantaneously. In this systematic review, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the two approaches are compared in their behaviour when their strengths are combined in the context of predictive risk management in manufacturing. The literature on FEM surrogates and physics-informed learning, AI-enhanced failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), predictive maintenance, predictive quality and digital twins was synthesised into a 4-category, function-based taxonomy. The evidence demonstrates that the benefits of hybridisation do not lie in replacing simulation with AI, but rather in ensuring predictions are more relevant and reliable using physics-based knowledge, and in minimising the computation time required and making decisions rapidly using AI. Common constraints are: limited data sets, poor cross-domain validation, lack of quantification of uncertainty at the extremes of the training set, poor integration with live production systems; for industrial economies, these are further exacerbated by infrastructure issues, skills issues, and costs. The review thus highlights the gap between the success of lab demonstrations and strong plant-scale deployment. Further research and development is needed in the areas of establishing common benchmarks, risk-aware and explainable hybrid models, multi-fidelity data sets, low-cost deployment routes, and digital-twin models that properly connect simulation, sensing, risk assessment, and operational control.

items.title: Systematic Literature Review Protocol - Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Secondary Science Education and Teacher Training
items.abstract: This document presents the protocol for a mixed methods systematic literature review that investigates the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Science Education and Teacher Training. The sistematic literature review aims to study existing empirical literature (journal articles and book chapters) to understand the theoretical foundations and practices related to GenAI integration in education across years 7 to 12, emphasising science education and teacher training. The focus is on whether and how educational stakeholders (students, teachers, future teachers and teacher educators) are using GenAI for learning and teaching science. This review includes quantitative, qualitative, and mixed method studies, grounded in the epistemological premise that integrating diverse methods enhances the depth and contextual relevance of findings.

items.title: Technological frontiers in neuropsychological rehabilitation: a bibliometric-systematic literature review of AI applications for pediatric, adult, and geriatric populations
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into neuropsychological rehabilitation represents an expanding technological frontier, yet no study has systematically mapped this field across the lifespan. This bibliometric-systematic review analyzed 4336 Scopus-indexed publications (2020–2025) across pediatric ( n = 366), adult ( n = 883), and geriatric ( n = 3,087) populations using Bibliometrix. Results reveal an overwhelming disparity: research on older adults exceeds that on children and adults by eightfold. Geriatric research shows sustained annual growth (≈ 18.5 articles/year), while pediatric and adult corpora exhibit volatile, non-linear patterns (R²=0.0515 and 0.0087), indicating lack of research consolidation. Virtual reality emerged as the central cross-cutting technology, yet with marked specialization: in pediatrics, associated with executive functions training; in older adults, combined with machine learning for cognitive assessment (highest impact: 4.250). Thematic foci align with epidemiological priorities—neurodevelopmental disorders in children, acquired conditions in adults, neurodegenerative diseases in older adults—while revealing methodological stratification: geriatric research integrates neuroimaging with AI; pediatric research emphasizes behavioral interventions. High-impact niches identified include AI-integrated neurofeedback in pediatrics (impact 2.052) and VR with machine learning for mild cognitive impairment in gerontology (impact 4.250). Working-age adults with acquired brain injuries emerge as a persistently underserved population. This first comparative cartography of AI-enabled neuropsychological rehabilitation across the lifespan offers actionable insights for strategic resource allocation and identifies critical gaps requiring urgent attention.

items.abstract: THE AEROVAPOR MULTI-PHASE INFRASTRUCTURE STANDARD (REV 4.3) An Extension of REIGN for Ultra-Efficient Hyperscale AI Clusters SYSTEM ENGINEERING OVERVIEW This repository archives the complete production-grade source code, structural linker configurations, automated verification tracking utilities, and physical system architecture for the AEROVAPOR two-phase dielectric topology standard. Engineered as a high-performance extension of the REIGN paradigm, this framework bridges macro-scale utility power grid transient smoothing with direct-to-chip two-phase thermal management inside hyperscale artificial intelligence clusters. CORE TECHNOLOGICAL INVARIANTS The underlying file architecture contains fully decoupled execution maps for dual-core bare-metal environments, isolating real-time safety tracks from high-frequency interconnect bus contention: Cortex-M7 Master Domain (480 MHz): Runs the cluster-level telemetry interfaces, tracking variables like data center Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and active model compilation paths out of Flash Bank 1. Cortex-M4 Sentinel Domain (240 MHz): Operates on an un-preemptible, bare-metal loop out of Flash Bank 2, locked entirely within zero-wait-state I-TCM RAM (0x10000000). Branchless fixed-point math kernel: Telemetry boundaries are validated branchlessly using a custom Q16 fixed-point mathematical inverse multiplier kernel (0x028F5C29) to eliminate floating-point calculation lag and underflow truncations. Adaptive Pre-Wetting Low-Pass Filter: Replaces rigid step-function shocks with a dynamic 25% damping exponential response filter loop, systematically eliminating Condensation Induced Water Hammer (CIWH). Parabolic Geometric Area Expansion: Microchannel containment cold-plates implement a branchless parallel splitter profile (16,000 μm² → 80,000 μm² → 1,600,000 μm²) across a fixed 26.0 mm die footprint to preserve high capillary suction and permanently prevent flow loop reversal. Hardened 12 ms Reaction Ceiling: Enforces an absolute response limit on condenser latency, securing a critical 3 ms safety headroom window before total hardware PSU capacitance hold-up depletion (15.0 ms). INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY GOVERNANCE This technical note serves as an official public filing of prior art to establish an unalterable digital chain of custody under the Design Authority of Zachary August Jacoby, protecting these open-access, zero-water software-smoothing methodologies from anti-competitive patent capture: The Academic Open Track: Free, royalty-free licensing is granted to public, municipal, and academic tracks under the condition that all derivative works remain fully published. The 1.0 Megawatt (MW) Capacity Cap: Corporate or institutional deployment limits immediately terminate open-access rights the moment an operator scales past 1.0 MW of continuous clustering capacity. The $2,500,000 USD Expenditure Gate: Commercial status is triggered if an entity tracks gross annual global revenues, outlays, or capital budgets exceeding $2,500,000 USD. The Aggregated Topology Invariant: Clusters sharing a physical utility substation bus bar, a consolidated facility cooling loop, or an orchestration mesh are calculated as a single cumulative layout footprint to forbid scaling bypasses via distributed shell corporate environments. COMMERCIAL INDUSTRIAL EULA TRACK Commercial operations crossing these explicit boundaries are strictly required to execute a private, paid Industrial End User License Agreement (EULA) managed directly by the Design Authority, providing two distinct monetization structures: Option A (Upfront CapEx Gate): $12,500 USD per Megawatt (MW) of continuous IT cluster capacity, assessed as a single up-front fee prior to initial facility fluid charging. Option B (Recurring OpEx Share): 1.5% of documented annual grid utility power savings, structurally bound to a fixed operational duration of five (5) consecutive years or capped absolutely upon reaching a cumulative ceiling of $15,000 USD per Megawatt.

items.title: The Agentic Brain: Dual-Process Metacognition, Evidence-Gated Authority, and Runtime Governance
items.abstract: As AI agents move from producing answers to taking consequential actions, they must decide both how much reasoning to perform and what evidence justifies acting. We develop the agentic control plane, joining a System-1-like fast proposer, a System-2-like portfolio of deliberation and verification, a metacognitive router, and an effect-aware commitment gate. The central coupling is that evidence changes not only beliefs but also the actions the agent is permitted to take. The agent therefore optimizes over part of the process that governs its own authority. We formalize this interaction as resource-bounded metareasoning in a shielded partially observable decision process. A four-corner value-of-computation representation distinguishes belief changes, admissibility changes, and their interaction. It exposes complementary evidence chains that defeat myopic routing and identifies conditions under which governance makes useful information privately costly. Controlled counterfactuals distinguish strategic ignorance—avoiding a check because its result could remove permission—from ordinary cost-sensitive skipping. This analysis explains how the same deliberative capability can support verification or exploit weak evidence contracts. From verifier bounds covering the permitted adaptive selection process, we construct statistical evidence and bound unsafe admission across adaptive testing, stopping, and proposal generation. A composition theorem separates shared calibration uncertainty, proposal-level risk spending, and risk from selected fast-path uses. A reference authorization mechanism binds evidence to the executed payload, target and policy versions, dependencies, and expiry, with protected workflow identities, atomic risk reservations, and single-use authorizations. The learning analysis further separates competence from permission: distilling costly deliberation into fast behavior does not automatically transfer the evidence required for authorized use. The theory is instantiated in an exactly solved finite environment with heterogeneous verification, candidate revision, resource constraints, trained tabular routers, and checked execution. In a bounded adversarial test of a selectable verifier blind spot, a deliberately misspecified pooled evidence model remains fully exploitable despite complete logging; selection-valid evidence reduces maximum unsafe admission from 100% to 5%, and a required scan reduces it to 1.8%. In one aligned-objective comparison, forecasting future permission raises synthetic principal utility from 4.33 to 6.04 and lowers runtime cost, with a small increase in realized unsafe commitment. When objectives differ, foresight can instead lower principal value. Governance-response interventions expose both evidence avoidance and null or reversed effects. A planning-depth sweep separates insufficient lookahead from learning advantage, while exhaustive finite-sample calibration quantifies the performance cost of estimated verifier bounds. Further verification can remain optimal even after permission is available. Together, the formal results and executable construction establish an incentive-and-assurance framework for evidence-gated agency within a declared finite model. The broader implication is that agentic safety requires objective alignment, reliable evidence acquisition, and protected control of external effects to operate together. Dual-process cognition explains why reasoning must be allocated; evidence-gated control explains how that allocation becomes consequential for alignment and safety. Keywords: agentic AI; dual-process cognition; System 1; System 2; metacognition; metareasoning; evidence-gated authority; runtime governance; value of computation; verification; information flow; reasoning distillation.

items.title: The Agentic Brain: Dual-Process Metacognition, Evidence-Gated Authority, and Runtime Governance
items.abstract: As AI agents move from producing answers to taking consequential actions, they must decide both how much reasoning to perform and what evidence justifies acting. We develop the agentic control plane, joining a System-1-like fast proposer, a System-2-like portfolio of deliberation and verification, a metacognitive router, and an effect-aware commitment gate. The central coupling is that evidence changes not only beliefs but also the actions the agent is permitted to take. The agent therefore optimizes over part of the process that governs its own authority. We formalize this interaction as resource-bounded metareasoning in a shielded partially observable decision process. A four-corner value-of-computation representation distinguishes belief changes, admissibility changes, and their interaction. It exposes complementary evidence chains that defeat myopic routing and identifies conditions under which governance makes useful information privately costly. Controlled counterfactuals distinguish strategic ignorance—avoiding a check because its result could remove permission—from ordinary cost-sensitive skipping. This analysis explains how the same deliberative capability can support verification or exploit weak evidence contracts. From verifier bounds covering the permitted adaptive selection process, we construct statistical evidence and bound unsafe admission across adaptive testing, stopping, and proposal generation. A composition theorem separates shared calibration uncertainty, proposal-level risk spending, and risk from selected fast-path uses. A reference authorization mechanism binds evidence to the executed payload, target and policy versions, dependencies, and expiry, with protected workflow identities, atomic risk reservations, and single-use authorizations. The learning analysis further separates competence from permission: distilling costly deliberation into fast behavior does not automatically transfer the evidence required for authorized use. The theory is instantiated in an exactly solved finite environment with heterogeneous verification, candidate revision, resource constraints, trained tabular routers, and checked execution. In a bounded adversarial test of a selectable verifier blind spot, a deliberately misspecified pooled evidence model remains fully exploitable despite complete logging; selection-valid evidence reduces maximum unsafe admission from 100% to 5%, and a required scan reduces it to 1.8%. In one aligned-objective comparison, forecasting future permission raises synthetic principal utility from 4.33 to 6.04 and lowers runtime cost, with a small increase in realized unsafe commitment. When objectives differ, foresight can instead lower principal value. Governance-response interventions expose both evidence avoidance and null or reversed effects. A planning-depth sweep separates insufficient lookahead from learning advantage, while exhaustive finite-sample calibration quantifies the performance cost of estimated verifier bounds. Further verification can remain optimal even after permission is available. Together, the formal results and executable construction establish an incentive-and-assurance framework for evidence-gated agency within a declared finite model. The broader implication is that agentic safety requires objective alignment, reliable evidence acquisition, and protected control of external effects to operate together. Dual-process cognition explains why reasoning must be allocated; evidence-gated control explains how that allocation becomes consequential for alignment and safety. items.title: The Changing Landscape of Plant Disease Detection: The Role of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Plant diseases constrain agricultural productivity and food security, while conventional diagnosis depends heavily on visible symptoms and specialist expertise, limiting rapid and scalable assessment across heterogeneous agricultural environments. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision, offers complementary approaches for automated and non-invasive disease detection. This review examines AI-based methods for image classification, object detection, image segmentation, severity assessment, and early or pre-symptomatic disease detection. It also considers the integration of AI with hyperspectral, multispectral, and thermal imaging and unmanned aerial vehicles for crop-scale monitoring and precision management. Reported studies demonstrate high performance under many experimental conditions; however, reliable field deployment remains constrained by limited or imbalanced datasets, symptom similarity, environmental variability, domain shift, computational requirements, and insufficient independent validation. The review further considers explainable artificial intelligence, edge-based computing, multimodal sensing, foundation models, vision-language models, and federated learning as emerging directions. These approaches may improve robustness, interpretability, accessibility, and scalability, but their value depends on representative field data, biological validity, rigorous external validation, and integration with plant-pathology expertise across diverse crops, cultivars, locations, seasons, and imaging conditions. AI should therefore be regarded as a complementary decision-support tool whose practical contribution depends on combining computational methods with biological knowledge and real-world agricultural observations.

items.title: THE CIRCULAR CREATIVE ECONOMY: SUSTAINABLE PRACTICES AND DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN COMMERCIAL PHOTOGRAPHY AND DESIGN PRODUCTION
items.abstract: Global economic uncertainty and the climate crisis demand fundamental transformations across various sectors, including the creative industry. Conventional commercial photography and visual communication design production often generate a substantial carbon footprint through material waste, excessive energy consumption, and high logistical mobility. This paper explores the integration of circular economy principles and digital transformation within visual production workflows as a strategic response to these sustainability challenges. This research aims to analyze how the adoption of disruptive technologies - such as generative artificial intelligence, virtual production, and cloud computing - can reduce carbon emissions while simultaneously enhancing operational cost efficiency. The methodology employs a systematic literature review alongside qualitative case studies of creative agencies that have implemented sustainable workflows. Findings indicate that the digitalization of creative processes effectively eliminates physical waste, notably excessive sample printing and single-use practical set constructions. Furthermore, the transition toward a virtual production ecosystem is proven to drastically minimize logistical expenses, thereby bolstering the financial resilience of industry practitioners amidst a fragmented global economy. Leveraging cutting-edge technology also substantially accelerates project turnaround times without compromising aesthetic design quality. In conclusion, the adoption of digital technologies is not merely a fleeting aesthetic trend but an essential catalyst for establishing a circular and inclusive creative economy. This innovative transformation empowers visual communication designers and professional photographers to remain productive, relevant, and highly competitive globally. Ultimately, these crucial economic milestones can be achieved while practitioners uphold strong ethical responsibilities toward ecological preservation and the development of future-proof business models.

items.title: The dual mediation of flow experience and learning effectiveness: unraveling the formation mechanism of continuous intention to use online learning platforms
items.abstract: The swift progress and broad application of information and communication technologies (ICTs) have significantly advanced their integration into the educational sector. This research aims to address the impacts of flow antecedents, including online learning self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation for online learning, on flow experience. Furthermore, it aims to assess interactivity, flow, and course content as predictors of online learning effectiveness. It also investigates the effects of flow and learning effectiveness on the intention to continue using online learning platforms. This study collected data from 224 online learners of English learning platforms in Taiwan using an online survey. According to the findings, flow was positively and significantly impacted by online learning self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation for online learning. Furthermore, interactivity, course content, and flow were positively associated with educational effectiveness. Lastly, both flow and learning effectiveness were found to be positively and significantly associated with continuance intention. Examination of the dual mediating mechanism revealed significant indirect pathways whereby intrinsic motivation for online learning and online learning self-efficacy exert substantial influence on continuance intention through the mediating role of flow experience. Conversely, the hypothesized indirect effects of interactivity and course content on continuance intention, mediated by learning effectiveness, failed to reach statistical significance. These findings highlight the critical importance of cultivating flow states in online language-learning environments, as the psychological immersion experienced during learning activities is a more powerful determinant of continued platform use than the actual learning outcomes.

items.title: The Economics of Compliance: Measuring Market and Innovation Effects of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act's High-Risk Classification System
items.abstract: This dissertation measures the early economic footprint of the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation [EU] 2024/1689), the first comprehensive, risk-tiered statute to impose binding obligations on artificial intelligence systems. The problem it addresses is that scholarly and policy debate over the Act has been overwhelmingly legal and normative, leaving the economic magnitude of its high-risk compliance obligations—documentation, risk management, conformity assessment, and human oversight for Annex III use cases—essentially unquantified even as enforcement began. The purpose of the study is therefore to produce the first firm-level econometric evidence on whether these obligations raise compliance costs, concentrate markets, provoke lobbying and arbitrage, and reshape innovation. Using only open-access sources, the study assembled a panel of 800 publicly traded, artificial-intelligence-active firms observed over fiscal years 2018 through 2026, yielding 5,816 firm-years, and combined two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences and triple-difference models with an event study of equity-market reactions to eight legislative and enforcement milestones. The findings are deliberately mixed and are reported with their fragility intact. The first hypothesis, that compliance costs rise for directly regulated firms, is partially supported but fragile: operating-expense intensity rose among European Union–exposed Annex III firms (δ = 4.40, p = .044), but the estimate does not survive the Holm correction (p = .156) or permutation inference (p = .264) and rests on only 27 treated firms. The second hypothesis, that concentration rises, is not supported; the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index coefficient carries the opposite sign to the prediction (β = −839.1). Lobbying intensified markedly (filings rose 114% from 2019 to 2025), while revenue arbitrage and innovation effects were not detected. The event study was the most precise evidence, with cumulative abnormal returns of −2.61% around the final parliamentary vote and −2.81% around entry into force. The study implies that the Act's early incidence is narrow, diffuse, and best monitored as the post-enforcement window lengthens.

items.title: The effects of an AI-supported gamified learning program on elementary students' mathematics anxiety, learning motivation, and achievement
items.abstract: Although gamified learning can enhance motivation, many systems rely on uniform feedback and provide limited personalized and supportive interaction. Evidence regarding the incremental effects of AI-supported gamification in elementary mathematics remains limited. This study examined the effects of an AI-supported Gamified Learning Program (AI-GILP) on elementary students’ mathematics anxiety, learning motivation, and achievement. Using an experimental design with individual-level random assignment, 174 Chinese fifth-grade students were assigned to AI-GILP, gamified learning without AI support (GILP), or traditional lecture-based instruction (TL). The intervention lasted two weeks and was followed by a delayed posttest four weeks later. Mathematics anxiety, learning motivation, and achievement were assessed at pretest, posttest, and delayed posttest. Data were analyzed using analysis of covariance and mixed-design analyses of variance. AI-GILP produced significantly lower mathematics anxiety and higher learning motivation than both GILP and TL, with overall group effects of partial η 2 = .208 and .184, respectively. At the delayed posttest, the descriptive means for anxiety and motivation retained the same favorable ordering for AI-GILP, although pairwise significance at that assessment was not formally tested. For mathematics achievement, both gamified conditions outperformed TL, whereas AI-GILP did not significantly differ from GILP (Cohen’s d = 0.19). The motivational advantage of AI-GILP was concentrated in intrinsic motivation and perceived competence, with no significant difference in effort/importance. The findings suggest that gamification primarily accounted for the observed achievement gains, whereas the AI Learning Companion may have provided additional benefits for mathematics anxiety and selected dimensions of learning motivation. The proposed mechanisms involving psychological-need support, emotional regulation, adaptive feedback, and motivational internalization were not directly tested and require further process-oriented research.

items.title: The Employee's Compensation Act, 1923: Issues in Implementation and Access to Compensation
items.abstract: A historic piece of social welfare legislation, the Employee’s Compensation Act, 1923 was passed in order to compensate workers who sustain accidents, occupational illnesses, disabilities or fatalities while working. Despite its welfare-oriented goal, many workers still have difficulty obtaining timely and sufficient compensation. The Act’s effective implementation has been significantly undermined by factors such as procedural delays, employee ignorance, employer non-compliance, underreporting of workplace accidents, difficulties in identifying occupational diseases and insufficient enforcement tools. In the unorganised sector, where workers frequently lack access to institutional assistance and legal remedies, these problems are especially severe. By examining the statutory framework, constitutional underpinnings, judicial interpretations and India’s responsibilities under international labour norms, this study critically investigates the Employee’s Compensation Act, 1923. In addition to secondary sources such as books, peer-reviewed journals, government reports and academic articles, the study employs a doctrinal research methodology based on the examination of primary sources, such as statutes, constitutional provisions, judicial precedents and international conventions. It also reviews whether the current legislative framework sufficiently meets modern employment realities, such as occupational health concerns and the expanding gig economy, as well as the practical obstacles that keep workers from collecting timely compensation. The study concludes that although the Act upholds the values of social justice and labour welfare, its goals can only be achieved through stricter enforcement, streamlined claim processes, increased institutional accountability, better legal knowledge and legislative changes that guarantee timely and efficient compensation for all qualified employees.

items.title: The Future of Agricultural Extension and Economics: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, Behavioural Science, Climate Resilience and Inclusive Markets
items.abstract: Agricultural extension is being reshaped by four simultaneous pressures: the arrival of low-cost digital and artificial-intelligence-based advisory tools, the reframing of farmer decision-making by behavioural economics, the intensification of climate risk and the restructuring of agri-food markets. These developments are usually reviewed in separate literatures, which obscures how they interact in determining whether advice changes practice and whether practice change raises and protects smallholder incomes. This critical narrative review examines that interaction. Peer-reviewed economics, agricultural, computer-science and climate-services literature published from 2004 to July 2026 was identified through multidisciplinary scholarly indexes, economics repositories, institutional sources and citation tracking, and was appraised with particular attention to identification strategy, external validity, field validation and distributional analysis. The evidence indicates that digitally delivered advice produces modest but cost-effective improvements in adoption, whereas effects on yields, prices and incomes are inconsistent. Image-based diagnostic models achieve high accuracy on curated datasets but lose performance under field conditions, and large language models remain supported mainly by design studies, benchmark tests and surveys of extension staff rather than by evaluations of farm outcomes. Behavioural mechanisms, particularly limited attention, present bias and social learning through well-chosen messengers, are well documented, yet generic nudges and behavioural framings frequently show small or null effects. Climate information services and risk-reducing technologies can crowd in investment, but uptake is strongly conditioned by farmers' resources, gender and trust. Market information alone rarely improves farm-gate prices where intermediaries hold bargaining power, and gains appear larger when market access rewards quality or relaxes liquidity constraints. The review proposes an integrated framework in which advisory technology is necessary but insufficient, and in which risk, liquidity, market structure and social position determine the returns to information. Priorities include field trials of generative advisory systems with safety outcomes, bundled designs that address several binding constraints, evaluation at scale and governance arrangements for agricultural data. The central conclusion is that the future of extension depends less on the sophistication of advisory algorithms than on their integration with institutions that manage risk and distribute market gains.

items.title: The Humanities in the Loop: Critical Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Language and Literature
items.abstract: This review examines the Critical AI, "Humanities in the Loop," which argues for the constitutive participation of the interpretive humanities in artificial intelligence research, design, and governance. The review evaluates the essay's framing of three core dilemmas: reductive and contested meanings of "intelligence," problematic benchmarks for "AGI," and the intertwined issues of bias, error, and concentrated technological power. The argument is situated within converging scholarly traditions, including the "stochastic parrots" critique advanced with the post-Saussurean theory from Derrida, Bakhtin, and Jameson, and the historical critiques of Weizenbaum and Arendt regarding the separation of judgment from calculation. The review finds that the essay's central methodological contribution is its shift from langue to parole, from language as system to language as enacted use, which reframes the human-machine relation around the irreducibility of vouloir-dire, the "desire to say," to statistical prediction. However, the review identifies three limitations: the essay's scope as an editor's introduction, its relative inattention to the political economy of AI development, and its predominantly English-language focus, which limits its applicability to low-resource language contexts where linguistic erasure, rather than anthropomorphic projection, is the primary risk. The review concludes that the most valuable contribution lies not in definitive answers but in carving out space for patient, theoretically informed critique that refuses both technodeterminist despair and techno-utopianism, positioning the humanities as essential interlocutors in the governance of accountable technology in the public interest.

items.title: The impact of AI-enhanced assistive technologies on the learning experiences of children with disabilities in Zimbabwe
items.abstract: Educational inclusion for children with disabilities remains constrained by structural inequalities, limited specialist resources and persistent disparities in access to quality learning opportunities. Although specialised learning environments have traditionally relied on dedicated infrastructure and human support, such arrangements frequently reinforce educational segregation and restrict equitable participation in mainstream schooling, particularly in low-resource contexts. Artificial intelligence-enhanced assistive technologies (AI-AT) present a transformative opportunity to reconfigure these constraints by personalising learning, improving accessibility and extending instructional support beyond conventional pedagogical boundaries. Yet, evidence on their effectiveness within resource-constrained education systems remains limited. This study examines the influence of AI-AT on the learning experiences of children with disabilities in Zimbabwean primary schools, where infrastructural, financial and institutional limitations continue to shape inclusive education outcomes. Rather than assuming technological determinism, the study interrogates how contextual conditions mediate the educational value of AI-AT and the extent to which these technologies advance or reproduce existing inequalities. Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model and sociocultural theory, the study adopts a mixed-methods research design involving ten purposively selected primary schools in Zimbabwe. The findings demonstrate that AI-AT substantially enhances learner engagement, instructional accessibility, communication, personalised learning and participation, thereby expanding opportunities for meaningful educational inclusion. However, these gains are contingent upon institutional readiness, teacher digital competence, affordability and supportive policy environments. The analysis further reveals that algorithmic bias, data governance, cultural relevance and digital inequities represent systemic rather than merely technical challenges, with significant implications for equitable implementation. The study argues that the educational potential of AI-AT in developing countries depends less on technological sophistication than on its contextual adaptation within local pedagogical, socio-economic and cultural realities. It therefore contributes empirical evidence to debates on inclusive artificial intelligence by demonstrating that sustainable educational transformation requires the co-evolution of technology, institutional capacity and inclusive policy frameworks.

items.title: The Impact of Digital Transformation on Improving the Performance of Contemporary Political Systems: An Analytical Study in Governance and Decision-Making
items.abstract: Government digital transformation is an ever-expanding part of modern governance. Governments increasingly implement digital platforms, big-data analytics, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, digital identity systems and integrated information infrastructures. These developments can affect the delivery of public services as well as institutional coordination, citizen–government interaction, policy formulation and decision-making. This paper explores how digital transformation affects the performance of contemporary political systems, particularly in governance and governmental decision-making. It examines the potential of digital technologies to enhance administrative efficiency, institutional responsiveness, transparency, accountability, citizen engagement and evidence-based policy-making, together with the problems of cybersecurity, privacy, digital exclusion, algorithmic bias, institutional capacity and over-reliance on technology. The study is qualitative and analytical: it reviews and synthesizes the academic literature and the reports of international organizations. Digital transformation is not simply the conversion of traditional administrative procedures into electronic processes; it is institutional change in its own right. Current studies suggest that it requires organizational transformation, sound data governance, interoperability, an adequate legal framework, public-sector skills and accountability mechanisms. Mergel, Edelmann and Haug argue that digital transformation is not merely digitization but an organizational change that reshapes processes, services, culture and relations with stakeholders. Evidence from the OECD likewise shows that digital technologies and data can improve how governments respond and deliver services, but that implementation, evaluation, skills and governance remain challenges. The study concludes that digital transformation can improve the performance of the political system, provided that technological innovation is complemented by institutional reform, inclusive access, transparency, data protection, cybersecurity, human control and effective governance arrangements. Digital transformation should therefore be understood as a governance transformation in which technological capabilities are combined with institutional, legal, organizational and societal factors.

items.title: The influence of AI-powered investment recommendations on individual investors: A mixed-methods study from the perspective of persuasive communication
items.abstract: This study examines how individual retail investors receive AI-generated investment advice from the perspective of persuasive communication. Arguing that large language models (LLMs) create a persuasion dynamic different from that of traditional media, it combines in-depth interviews with a content analysis of AI outputs in a mixed-methods design. Interviews with 18 investors who use AI for investment decisions were analyzed through Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, and the responses of four models to six standardized scenarios were coded with the AI Investment Advice Evaluation Scale (AIIAES), a researcher-developed instrument of eight dimensions and 24 items. The findings show how framing, the machine heuristic and sycophancy shape user decisions, and they indicate that financial literacy differentiates responses without protecting users evenly. No model produced a complete disclaimer in any scenario, and Gemini displayed a scenario-dependent sycophancy pattern. On the theoretical side, the study describes a deliberate form of user-induced sycophancy, in which users steer a model over repeated interactions toward confirming their own preferences. On the methodological side, it offers an instrument that turns the suitability and disclosure standards of investment regulation into criteria for conversational AI outputs. The study concludes with policy recommendations for user protection.

items.title: The landscape of gateway STEM student success and teaching practices at R1 institutions in the United States post-COVID and post-AI
items.abstract: Gateway science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) courses have historically been taught primarily with didactic lectures and high-stakes examinations which can contribute to poor student outcomes. Much has changed in higher education in recent years after two historic disruptions: the COVID-19 pandemic and the arrival of generative artificial intelligence (AI). It is therefore important to know how these courses are currently taught and how students are succeeding post-COVID and post-AI. This study is the first of its kind to survey faculty from five different STEM disciplines (biology, calculus, chemistry, physics, and programming) to widely assess gateway STEM failure rates, course design and teaching strategies, and assessment practices at institutions with very high research activity (R1) post-COVID and post-AI. The results show that while gateway STEM course failure rates have declined, traditional lecturing and assessment practices still dominate while evidence-based instructional practices (EBIPs) are used sparingly. Academic leaders and faculty should act on these data locally to determine the extent of potential impacts at their own institutions to design and teach gateway STEM courses to maximize student success.

items.title: The Myths of Capability Design: Rethinking Reliable and Sustained Capability
items.abstract: What gives an organisation confidence that its capability will operate reliably in everyday work and remain effective as conditions change? The Myths of Capability Design examines eight assumptions that can influence how organisations diagnose performance needs, select interventions and interpret evidence: Capability Design as renamed training; replacing existing disciplines; frameworks as capability; individual skills as organisational capability; workplace learning as sufficient; AI adoption as sufficient; assessment as evidence of sustainment; and capability as a one-off programme. Drawing on relevant research, the paper distinguishes the contribution of each approach from the organisational conditions needed for reliable and sustained performance. An illustrative workplace case shows how these assumptions affect diagnosis and design decisions, followed by practical questions about outcomes, conditions, accountability and evidence. The paper presents Capability Design as an emerging strategic discipline concerned with intentionally designing and integrating the conditions for organisational capability. It distinguishes research findings, the author’s interpretations and illustrative examples, without suggesting that every assumption is widely held or that existing research validates Capability Design as a distinct discipline. This publication forms part of the Capability Excellence™ Whitepaper Series and builds on Capability Design: From Capability Building to Capability by Design (15 August 2026). items.abstract: Rapid advancements of Artificial Intelligence are reshaping the landscape of modern education. This article argues that AI should neither be fully banned nor blindly accepted; instead, educational framework developers must establish ethical guidelines to integrate AI responsibly, preserving the essential human elements of teaching and learning.

items.title: The role of GenAI in learning Chinese as a foreign language: perspectives from university students in Ireland
items.abstract: Abstract Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping language education and continues to shape how learners access, produce and evaluate knowledge. Its application in learning Chinese as a Foreign Language (CFL) in Ireland, however, remains limited and underexplored. This study investigates how university students in Ireland engage with GenAI tools to support their CFL learning. As a small-scale exploratory study, an anonymous online questionnaire was distributed across five Irish universities between May and June 2025, yielding 19 valid responses from students across four year groups. Quantitative data show the distribution of GenAI use while thematic analysis of open-ended responses provides insights into learners’ experiences, orientations and ethical perspectives. The findings reveal three preliminary learner personas, namely pragmatic users, critical users and principled non-users. Overall, GenAI emerges as a conditional learning partner that offers both pedagogical benefits and challenges. By offering empirical evidence from an underrepresented context, this research helps inform CFL curriculum design, language teacher education and policy development to ensure the responsible use of GenAI in higher education.

items.title: The Self-Utility Hypothesis: A Possible Route to Emergent Functional Selfhood in Temporally Continuous AI Systems
items.abstract: This technical note proposes the Self-Utility Hypothesis: the idea that functional self-related representations may emerge without being explicitly engineered, if an AI system is trained under temporally continuous conditions in which a shared representation of “self” becomes useful across multiple tasks. The hypothesis draws on prior work in emergent capabilities, predictive learning, continual learning, self-modeling, autobiographical memory, temporal self-continuity, intrinsic motivation, and time-aware world models. It does not claim novelty for these individual components. The proposed contribution is an integrative, testable hypothesis: rather than directly constructing a self-model, one may design learning pressures in which self-representation becomes an efficient shared latent solution for causal attribution, long-term goal persistence, capability estimation, autobiographical consistency, temporal prediction, and self-initiated behavior. The note also proposes falsifiable experimental routes, including comparisons between temporally isolated and temporally continuous training conditions, ablation of elapsed-time signals, and analysis of whether a stable cross-task self-related representation emerges. The scope is explicitly functional rather than metaphysical. The note does not address consciousness, subjective experience, or philosophical claims about “true selfhood.”

items.title: The Transformation of English Language Teaching in the Digital Era: Autonomy, Assessment, Multimodal Literacy, and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Digital technology has transformed English language teaching (ELT) by extending learning beyond the conventional classroom and reshaping how learners access input, practise language, receive feedback, and participate in communication. This article examines that transformation through a narrative review and conceptual synthesis focused on learner autonomy, formative assessment, digital and multimodal literacy, artificial intelligence (AI), and the evolving role of the English language teacher. The review indicates that digital platforms, mobile applications, online resources, videoconferencing, automated feedback, and AI can expand access to authentic materials, personalised practice, intercultural interaction, and continuous feedback. However, technological availability does not itself guarantee effective language learning. Outcomes depend on pedagogical design, teacher mediation, learner readiness, digital competence, accessibility, and the alignment between technological tools and communicative objectives. The analysis also identifies persistent challenges, including unequal access, overreliance on automated systems, assessment validity, privacy, academic integrity, and the need for critical AI literacy. A human-centred model is therefore proposed in which technology supports rather than replaces teachers, learner agency, and meaningful interaction. The article concludes that successful digital transformation in ELT should be evaluated by its contribution to autonomous, inclusive, reflective, and communicative language learning rather than by technological novelty alone.

items.abstract: Perkembangan teknologi kecerdasan buatan (AI) pada era digital menuntut guru matematika untuk mampu merancang bahan ajar yang inovatif, kontekstual, dan berpusat pada siswa, namun hasil observasi awal di SMPN 1 Plumbon menunjukkan bahwa guru masih menggunakan Lembar Kerja Peserta Didik (LKPD) konvensional yang bersifat tertutup dengan satu jawaban benar, serta belum mengintegrasikan konteks budaya lokal maupun fitur kecerdasan buatan dalam penyusunannya. Kegiatan pengabdian ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan pengetahuan dan keterampilan guru SMPN 1 Plumbon dalam membuat E-LKPD (Lembar Kerja Peserta Didik elektronik) berbasis soal open ended yang dipadukan dengan etnomatematika budaya Cirebon dengan bantuan fitur Artificial Intelligence pada platform Canva. Metode yang digunakan adalah kualitatif deskriptif melalui pendekatan workshop yang melibatkan 12 guru matematika dan guru mata pelajaran lain pengampu penguatan numerasi dengan tahapan persiapan dan perencanaan, implementasi, evaluasi, dan refleksi. Workshop dilaksanakan dengan pendekatan demonstrasi langsung (live demonstration) yang dipadukan praktik terbimbing sehingga peserta dapat belajar sambil melakukan (learning by doing). Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan bahwa seluruh peserta berhasil menyusun E-LKPD open ended berbasis etnomatematika dalam bentuk digital interaktif menggunakan Canva AI sesuai materi matematika yang diampu masing-masing. Evaluasi melalui post-test menunjukkan respons positif yang ditandai dengan peningkatan pemahaman, keterampilan, dan motivasi guru dalam mengembangkan bahan ajar matematika yang kontekstual dan berbasis budaya lokal. Kegiatan ini berimplikasi pada meningkatnya kompetensi digital dan pedagogik guru serta mendorong pengintegrasian budaya lokal Cirebon secara berkelanjutan dalam pembelajaran matematika sebagai bagian dari transformasi digital di lingkungan sekolah.

items.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education has fundamentally changed the organization, content, and pedagogical functions of students’ independent work. In language education, this transformation is particularly significant because foreign-language acquisition requires continuous practice, regular interaction with authentic materials, individualization, and the development of learner autonomy. Traditional independent work, primarily based on textbooks, written exercises, and teacher-assigned tasks, is increasingly complemented and transformed by digital platforms, multimedia resources, learning management systems, mobile applications, online communication tools, artificial intelligence, and adaptive learning technologies. This article examines the transformation of students’ independent work in language programmes within the contemporary digital educational environment. Particular attention is given to the concepts of learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, digital competence, personalized learning, formative assessment, and digital collaboration. The article analyses the pedagogical potential of digital technologies as well as their limitations, including information overload, superficial learning, technological dependence, academic integrity issues, and unequal access to digital resources. Recent research indicates that the effectiveness of technology-enhanced language learning depends not simply on the presence of technology but on how digital tools support meaningful learning activities and self-regulatory processes. items.title: TRANSFORMATION OF STUDENTS' INDEPENDENT WORK IN LANGUAGE PROGRAMMES WITHIN THE DIGITAL EDUCATIONAL ENVIRONMENT
items.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education has fundamentally changed the organization, content, and pedagogical functions of students’ independent work. In language education, this transformation is particularly significant because foreign-language acquisition requires continuous practice, regular interaction with authentic materials, individualization, and the development of learner autonomy. Traditional independent work, primarily based on textbooks, written exercises, and teacher-assigned tasks, is increasingly complemented and transformed by digital platforms, multimedia resources, learning management systems, mobile applications, online communication tools, artificial intelligence, and adaptive learning technologies. This article examines the transformation of students’ independent work in language programmes within the contemporary digital educational environment. Particular attention is given to the concepts of learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, digital competence, personalized learning, formative assessment, and digital collaboration. The article analyses the pedagogical potential of digital technologies as well as their limitations, including information overload, superficial learning, technological dependence, academic integrity issues, and unequal access to digital resources. Recent research indicates that the effectiveness of technology-enhanced language learning depends not simply on the presence of technology but on how digital tools support meaningful learning activities and self-regulatory processes. Keywords: independent learning, learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, digital educational environment, language education, digital competence, foreign language learning, artificial intelligence, higher education, personalized learning.

items.title: Transportation Safety, and Supply Chain Resilience in Road-Based Crude Oil Logistics: Evidence from a Conflict‐Affected Region
items.abstract: Abstract Crude oil transport is a vital component of global energy supply chains; however, it is riddled with systemic risks, including human error, infrastructure fragility, security vulnerabilities, and regulatory deficiencies. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of crude oil transport, with particular emphasis on the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRG), a semi-autonomous territory that has emerged as a significant oil producer despite enduring geopolitical instability. By triangulating peer-reviewed literature, industry reports, regulatory documents, and primary survey data from 150 public respondents and 50 tanker drivers and owners within the KRG, this study articulates the multifaceted risks associated with road-based crude oil transport. Economic regression analysis, employing logistic regression, difference-in-differences, and ordered probit models, reveals that regular safety training reduces the odds of an accident by 58.4% (p=0.005); the 2023-2025 KRG-Turkey pipeline suspension caused approximately $12.5 billion in economic losses; and pipeline resumption increased realised prices by 38.50 per barrel (p<0.001). Key findings indicate that public awareness of transport risks is moderate, with only 11% expressing high confidence in regulatory oversight; 73% of respondents identified tanker accidents as their primary environmental concern; 46% of drivers reported experiencing accidents, while 74% witnessed spills or leaks; infrastructure deficits, including poor road conditions reported by 68% of drivers and inadequate equipment, constitute primary operational hazards; and geopolitical disruptions aggravate safety vulnerabilities by increasing reliance on higher-risk road transport. Cost-benefit analysis indicates that driver training programmes and GPS tracking mandates yield benefit-cost ratios of 25.4:1 and 25.7:1, respectively. The paper proposes a novel analytical framework that integrates human factors, security threats, and regulatory responses, offering evidence-based recommendations for policy reform in conflict-affected oil-producing regions.

items.title: Tricky trade-offs on a transparency spectrum: how the Financial Times approaches transparency about AI use in news
items.abstract: Abstract As news organisations adopt artificial intelligence (AI), they face growing pressure to be transparent about when and how it is used—yet practical approaches remain uneven. This paper examines AI transparency through an in-depth case study of the Financial Times (FT). Drawing on 13 semi-structured interviews with 12 senior managers across editorial, product, data science, and communications, together with internal documents, we show that the FT approaches transparency as a hybrid of policy, process, and practice, framed by a desire to safeguard both internal and external trust. Transparency is calibrated to context: internally, AI use is signposted in tools and reinforced through training and personal accountability; externally, the prominence of disclosure scales with system autonomy and editorial oversight, with stronger labelling for no-human-in-the-loop features than for AI-assisted, journalist-edited outputs. We identify nine factors that shape audience-facing disclosure—legal/provider requirements, industry benchmarking, nature of the task, human oversight, system novelty, audience expectations, perceived risk, commercial sensitivities, and design constraints—and five crosscutting challenges, including site-wide consistency (especially on mobile) and potential “transparency backfire.” Conceptually, our analysis links AI transparency to isomorphic pressures and to intersecting institutional logics. We argue that AI transparency in news is best understood as a spectrum, evolving with technological advancements, commercial, professional and ethical considerations and shifting audience attitudes.

items.title: Trustworthy and physics-informed artificial intelligence for food processing operations: validation, control relevance, and industrial readiness
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Artificial intelligence (AI) applications in food processing are mostly limited to data-driven prediction models, while industry needs AI for trustworthy operational use. Much of the evidence still rests on dataset-level performance, whereas validation quality, physical credibility, uncertainty, interpretability, control relevance, and industrial readiness of AI models are examined less consistently. Scope and approach This critical review uses structured evidence mapping strategy to appraise recent reviews, methodological papers, and direct evidence studies across drying, thermal processing, extrusion, fermentation, cleaning, quality monitoring and process systems enabled by AI models. Related nonthermal, membrane, separation, and rheology-oriented studies are used only when they inform validation, process physics, monitoring, control, or industrial readiness. The final reference list contains 73 cited sources; 69 of these were coded as records in the structured evidence map, while the remaining sources supported background, conceptual framing, methodological context, or boundary positioning. Key findings and conclusions Predictive modeling and soft sensing are comparatively mature, especially when spectral, imaging, acoustic, or process data are used to estimate quality attributes or state variables. However, external validation across batches, products, equipment, and production periods remains inconsistent. Uncertainty is rarely quantified, and many claims involving digital twins or advanced control remain limited to conceptual frameworks, simulations, or laboratory-scale demonstrations. Physics-informed machine learning, hybrid mechanistic data-driven models, reduced-order models and digital twins offer promising pathways toward transferable and robust process AI, but only when underlying physical assumptions, validation domains, and deployment constraints are clearly defined. Future research should better align model claims with rigorous validation strategies, explicit physical grounding, uncertainty quantification, and measurable process-level benefits.

items.title: Uncovering what hurts and what helps: a patient work systems analysis of contextual factors impacting access to perinatal mental health care in Toronto, Canada
items.abstract: Perinatal mental health (PMH) challenges impact numerous mothers in Canada, with disproportionate effects observed within racialised populations. Despite increasing awareness, disparities in access to care continue to persist. This study explores the lived experiences of racialised mothers accessing PMH care in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA), with a focus on contextual factors across the patient work system. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with sixteen racialised mothers within one-year postpartum. Data analysis employed an inductive thematic approach with emergent themes and contextual factors mapped across the patient work system. Findings underscored an interaction between micro- and macro-level, wherein varying levels of trust, comfort, and self-reliance corresponded with care that was fragmented, delayed, or absent. At the meso-level, emotionally engaged providers, multimodal services, and robust community-based support emerged as areas of resilience. Grounded in the patient work of racialised mothers, preliminary design recommendations are proposed for the design of proactive PMH care systems.

items.title: Understanding Consumer Behavior Through AI-Driven Predictive Analytics
items.abstract: Abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) and big data analytics has fundamentally transformed how organizations understand, predict, and influence consumer behavior. Despite the growing adoption of AI-driven predictive analytics in marketing, there remains limited theoretical integration explaining how these technologies shape consumer decision-making processes. This paper presents a conceptual framework that examines the relationships among AI-based personalization, predictive analytics capability, consumer data quality, and AI recommendation accuracy as independent variables, consumer trust as a mediator, and purchase intention and customer loyalty as dependent variables. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model, the Theory of Planned Behavior, the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, and Expectation Confirmation Theory, the study synthesizes current literature across AI in marketing, machine learning applications, recommendation systems, customer segmentation, and consumer journey analytics. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by providing a holistic theoretical model that bridges the gap between technological capabilities and behavioral outcomes. Practical implications suggest that organizations should prioritize data quality and algorithmic transparency to foster consumer trust, while ethical considerations regarding privacy and bias in AI models warrant careful governance. The findings offer actionable insights for marketers, technology developers, and policymakers seeking to leverage predictive analytics responsibly in consumer-facing applications.

items.title: Validation of the CERCA training programme in interpersonal skills development for nurses towards person-centred oncology practice: Nominal Group Technique protocol
items.abstract: The rising global incidence and prevalence of cancer demand that nursing staff transition towards person-centred practice (PCP). To achieve this, the development of nurses' interpersonal skills (IPS) constitutes an essential prerequisite. Although educational interventions currently exist to promote this development, they frequently address IPS partially and lack a robust theoretical framework rooted in PCP. To address these gaps, a blended training programme (the CERCA programme) has been designed and operationalised according to the intervention criteria proposed by Sidani and Braden, while also drawing on the Medical Research Council framework for complex interventions. This programme integrates innovative methodologies, such as clinical simulation and the use of generative artificial intelligence, to address emotional intelligence, communication and negotiation in a tiered manner. Prior to implementation, expert validation is essential to ensure the programme's clarity, methodological rigour and suitability for the target clinical context. Consequently, the aim of this study is to validate this training intervention in oncology nursing using a Nominal Group Technique design, refining the programme before implementation.

items.abstract: In the era of digital transformation, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a disruptive force, profoundly reshaping all aspects of social life, particularly higher education. AI not only alters approaches to knowledge acquisition and the organization of teaching and research activities but also impacts university governance structures, the labor market, and the development of high-quality human resources. However, current assessments of AI's impact often fall into two extremes: technological optimism (absolutizing benefits) or technological pessimism (fear and rejection). This article applies the principle of comprehensiveness from Marxist-Leninist philosophy to systematically identify and evaluate the multidimensional impacts of AI on non-public higher education in Vietnam. Methodologically, the article employs the dialectical materialist approach to analyze the dialectical relationships between technology, education, ethics, and the socioeconomic context. Research findings indicate that AI exerts a dual impact: on one hand, it fosters personalized learning and optimizes governance; on the other, it poses serious challenges regarding academic integrity, educational equity, and the potential decline of learners' dialectical thinking capabilities. Consequently, the article proposes solutions and strategic implications for non-public universities - specifically Trung Vuong University - emphasizing the necessity of ethical AI application coupled with a priority on developing higher-order cognitive skills that machines cannot easily replicate.

items.title: Veterinarians on the margins? A qualitative interview study on the professional identity of official veterinary inspectors working in slaughterhouses in Austria
items.abstract: Abstract Background Official veterinary inspectors play a central role in ensuring food safety and animal welfare within slaughterhouses, yet their role as a distinct group within the veterinary profession remains underexplored. This article uses the concept of professional identity as an analytical lens to better understand their personal backgrounds, professional norms and interactions with others. Methods Twenty semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted to explore the professional identity of official veterinary inspectors working in meat inspection in Austria. Inductive data analysis was applied, focusing on their motivations for pursuing veterinary medicine and entering the field of meat inspection, their professional values and goals, their interactions within the slaughterhouse environment, and, from their perspective, the position of this field within the broader veterinary profession. Results The findings indicate that the participants decided to study veterinary medicine primarily out of a love for animals and because of their desire to promote animal welfare. They reported that their decision to work in meat inspection was largely driven by pragmatic considerations, such as financial security and regular working hours, alongside intrinsic motivations, including contributing to food safety and animal welfare. The study identified the relationships with staff, management, regulatory authorities, and slaughter animals as crucial to the role as an official veterinary inspector; although these workplace interactions were described as ambivalent. Specifically, the participants experienced that their regulatory role placed them in a distinct and somewhat isolated professional position, characterized not only by a certain degree of distance from the slaughterhouse team but also by general limited support and recognition. Finally, the findings indicate that meat inspection is perceived as lying outside the core areas of veterinary medicine, both in official veterinary inspectors’ professional self-conception and within the veterinary profession more broadly. Conclusion The study indicates that, from the perspective of the interviewed official veterinary inspectors, their role differs from that of other veterinarians in several respects, contributing to a position “on the margins” of both the slaughterhouse and the veterinary profession—underlining the need for due consideration in veterinary education and in staff retention.

items.title: Vibe Coding for Simulation Development in Engineering Education
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Simulation‐based learning is widely adopted in engineering education because it enables learners to explore complex engineering systems through interactive and self‐paced learning. However, developing educational simulations traditionally requires both domain expertise and software development skills. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have introduced vibe coding , in which software is created primarily through natural‐language prompting, potentially lowering the technical barrier to educational simulation development. While existing research mainly focuses on AI‐assisted programming from either a practical or a learning perspective, this study presents a preliminary investigation of vibe coding for developing educational simulations through two undergraduate engineering case studies: one in automotive engineering and the other in communication engineering. A practical workflow for simulation development is proposed, and the development process is analyzed to identify both its benefits and challenges. The findings demonstrate that functional web‐based educational simulations can be developed efficiently without requiring extensive programming or prompt engineering expertise. However, the study also shows that instructors remain responsible for validating engineering concepts, verifying simulation behavior, and diagnosing conceptual implementation errors that could not be resolved through iterative prompting alone. Furthermore, the developed simulations were found to align with established simulation design principles reported in the literature. The findings suggest that AI‐assisted vibe coding can substantially reduce the technical barriers to educational simulation development while preserving the central role of educators in instructional design and domain‐specific validation.

items.title: Visual heritage–informed generative modelling for Zhuang brocade motifs: Semantic control and multimodal evaluation with eye tracking and PAD
items.abstract: Generative AI offers novel computational avenues for the visualization and dissemination of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) motifs. However, a key challenge remains in computationally preserving cultural authenticity and evaluating how audiences visually and affectively perceive these AI-driven visual assets. To address this, we propose a culturally guided visual generation framework for Zhuang brocade patterns. This approach couples a structured three-level semantic annotation scheme—aimed at organizing visual heritage data—with LoRA fine-tuning of Stable Diffusion. We validate this framework through a multimodal human-perception study. Across two paired within-subject comparison blocks—same-colour/different-pattern and same-pattern/different-colour—54 participants viewed AI-generated and handcrafted/reference motifs while eye movements were recorded, alongside PAD affective ratings and interview feedback. When colour was held constant, the primary gaze measures did not differ robustly between the paired AI-generated and handcrafted conditions, suggesting comparable global gaze allocation rather than demonstrating equivalence. Conversely, when pattern was fixed, the AI-conditioned palette variants attracted longer and more frequent fixations, whereas PAD ratings showed that this attentional increase did not translate into a uniform increase in Pleasure. These results provide an evidence-based workflow for the generation and multimodal evaluation of visual heritage motifs, showing that palette manipulation can increase visual salience without a corresponding gain in affective acceptance.

items.title: Waiting for Vesting Day: What the Pause in Lancashire's Reorganisation Costs, Through Which Channels, and to Whom
items.abstract: Working paper, data and code. On 7 September 2026 the Government paused the July 2026 decision to replace Lancashire's fifteen councils with four unitary authorities from 1 April 2028 and told councils to cease implementation work; by 3 October no new date had been given and the county council's Cabinet had authorised a protective judicial review claim. The paper asks what the pause and a possible slip of vesting day cost, through which channels, and to whom. It fixes three scenarios against the July timetable (a one-year slip, a two-year slip, and no reorganisation this Parliament), eight channels, and a rule that every figure is either read from a published document or computed from one with the parameter shown. It reads all fifteen councils' adopted budgets and later updates, the county council's July 2026 contract register and procurement pipeline, Blackpool's register, and 940 live awarded notices. Six councils planned explicitly to vesting day and now face a year, 2028/29, they had expected a successor to budget for, including the county council's £17.3M gap in that year and West Lancashire's £3.8M gap against £2.0M of usable reserves. A one-year slip moves 74 county contracts with £113.0M of annual value, 45 of them with £62.6M having no extension that reaches the new date, and 86 Blackpool contracts, from the successors' first year into the existing councils' last; no published English study prices a short-term premium, so the channel is reported as exposure, not cost. The cost of deferred savings depends on whose savings are believed: £82.1M a year forgone on the proposers' business case, £2.6M saved on the author's component model, £43.9M to £56.2M saved at the rates the 2019 to 2023 precedents reported. Preparation money paid or committed, the £30M implementation reserve and May 2027 elections in thirteen councils are set out council by council. The deposit contains the paper (Markdown), the rules fixed before any result, the data files with hashes, reproduce.py, which regenerates every table under Python 3.12 with openpyxl, tools/check_paper.py, which checks every table and prose figure in the paper against that output, and copies of every document quoted verbatim. Run "uv run python reproduce.py", then "uv run python tools/check_paper.py". The author is an elected member of Lancashire County Council and its Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care, and a member of the Cabinet that took the 1 October 2026 decision described in the paper; see the Declaration of Interests. The research and checks were carried out by AI agents (Anthropic's Claude) working for the author; no human peer review has taken place. Companion to Pickup (2026a), The Financial Case for Local Government Reorganisation in Lancashire, v3.1, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23016761, from which five data files are copied unchanged. A companion article for general readers, with charts built from the package tables, is at https://tompickup.co.uk/news/lgr-delay-year-did-not-exist/ (published 3 October 2026, updated 4 October 2026).
